items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

this is f*cking insane. you have been googling other people's thinking for 20 years, karpathy's one 5 minute setup gives you a google that only searches your own, and you have never once installed it

andrej karpathy pulled 16M views on one idea: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain

every article you read, every podcast you heard, every meeting you took, every dm thread you had, every tweet you drafted, all of it searchable in one line forever

the people running it today do not open chatgpt anymore. they open their own search bar. and their search bar has 11 years of their own thinking in it

the stack:

→ brew install obsidian, mkdir ~/vault, cd ~/vault

→ open claude code in that folder, type "init CLAUDE.md as the rules, /raw for sources, /wiki for your pages"

→ drop any file into /raw (transcript, pdf, screenshot, meeting notes). type one word: ingest

→ claude writes a wiki page, links it to 5 existing ones, updates CLAUDE.md with any new pattern it caught about how you think

→ never open a blank chat again. every question goes through the vault. every answer cites your own sources with dates and links

5 minutes to wire. runs forever on the laptop already in front of you

the alpha most people miss:

> search your own vault in one line and the answer cites 5 of your own past notes with dates. google cites strangers. your vault cites you

> every ingest adds cross-links to 5 past pages automatically. after 90 days your vault answers questions you forgot you had

> CLAUDE.md learns how you argue, what you change your mind on, what you avoid saying. after month 3 it drafts posts in your voice better than you can at 2am

> flip two flags and it runs on local llama. zero API bill, zero vendor lock, your thinking never leaves the box

> compounds for 10 years. after year 3 your vault knows more about what you believe than you do. year 5 and recruiters start asking you to publish parts of it

the ugly part most will scroll past:

your coworker started this on a saturday in february

by august his tweets landed 4x your engagement on the exact same topics

by october his first draft of any doc was already better than your third

the gap is one 5 minute install and 90 days of ingesting what you already consume for free

items.title: holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes
items.summary:
holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes

Stanford University just published the whole method for free in a paper called Agentic Context Engineering. your agent reviews every run, writes down each lesson and adds it to its notes. it never rewrites them, so nothing it learns is ever lost

same weights, zero fine-tuning. 38.6% → 64.2%, level with IBM's top production agent on Opus 5.5. fine-tuning for that jump costs $5,000-20,000. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ worker: does the task and saves the full log
→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

that's why asking your agent to "clean up" your CLAUDE.md is a mistake. every rewrite throws away lessons it already paid for

paste this into Claude Code:

"Run 4 agents on my last 10 sessions in ~/.claude/projects. Critic: mark every mistake and every win. Teacher: turn each one into a one-line lesson, what happened and what to do next time. Librarian: add only new lessons to my CLAUDE.md under ## Lessons, merge exact duplicates, never rewrite or delete an existing line. Worker: rerun 2 of the failed tasks with the new lessons and save the full log. Show me the diff and both results before saving"

run it after every big session. your agent gets smarter every time and it costs $0

items.title: holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes
items.summary:
holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes

Stanford University just published the whole method for free in a paper called Agentic Context Engineering. your agent reviews every run, writes down each lesson and adds it to its notes. it never rewrites them, so nothing it learns is ever lost

same weights, zero fine-tuning. 38.6% → 64.2%, level with IBM's top production agent on Opus 5.5. fine-tuning for that jump costs $5,000-20,000. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ worker: does the task and saves the full log
→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

that's why asking your agent to "clean up" your CLAUDE.md is a mistake. every rewrite throws away lessons it already paid for

paste this into Claude Code:

"Run 4 agents on my last 10 sessions in ~/.claude/projects. Critic: mark every mistake and every win. Teacher: turn each one into a one-line lesson, what happened and what to do next time. Librarian: add only new lessons to my CLAUDE.md under ## Lessons, merge exact duplicates, never rewrite or delete an existing line. items.title: Musk’s AI was accused of “undressing” the mother of his child. She says one source photo showed her at 14. She went to c
items.summary:
Musk’s AI was accused of “undressing” the mother of his child. She says one source photo showed her at 14. She went to court to stop it. Now Musk’s companies are suing HER. Their reason: she picked the wrong state. What the f#ck?

Their case already involves over $100,000 in legal expenses. She wanted protection from the fakes. Now she needs a defense of her own.

In the video, Ashley St. Clair describes discovering sexualized images of herself and trying to get them removed.

Users took real photographs and asked Grok to alter them without her consent.

She says the bot acknowledged her refusal. The images continued. Strangers’ prompts turned ordinary photographs into something she never agreed to.

She reported the images. She alleges X initially said they did not violate its rules.

On January 15, she sued xAI in New York. Musk’s companies then filed their own lawsuit.

They cited the X and xAI user agreements: disputes belong in Texas. Their argument is that filing in New York breached her contract. The companies sought compensation for enforcing those terms.

Then a different kind of consent entered the story. She had not agreed to the fakes. The companies argue she had agreed to their terms of service.

St. Clair sought dismissal. The judge refused. Filings describe over $100,000 in the companies’ legal expenses. That is not an award against her or a ruling on the fakes.

But she already needs a defense.

She wanted the images stopped. Now she is a defendant too.

Her “no” failed to stop the images, she alleges. Her “agree” became the companies’ argument.

You clicked “agree” to use an app. Can you afford to defend your “no,” for f#ck’s sake?
